ai.definition: Regulatory Tech (RegTech) platforms are software solutions designed to help organizations meet regulatory requirements efficiently. These platforms leverage technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and blockchain to automate compliance processes, enhance transparency, and reduce the risk of non-compliance.
ai.howItWorks: RegTech platforms typically use AI for data analysis and pattern recognition to ensure that financial transactions comply with regulatory standards. Blockchain technology is employed to create immutable records, providing a transparent audit trail. These systems can integrate with existing enterprise resource planning (ERP) and other business management software to streamline processes.
ai.problemSolved: RegTech platforms address the challenges of manual compliance reporting, which are time-consuming, error-prone, and costly. They help organizations in financial services meet regulatory requirements more efficiently while maintaining transparency and accountability.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and deploying software applications that incorporate AI algorithms, blockchain technology, and other relevant technologies. This process requires skilled developers, data scientists, and cybersecurity experts.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the platform architecture, integrating various technologies (AI, blockchain), testing the system for accuracy and security, and ensuring compliance with regulatory standards during development.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include software development costs, ongoing maintenance and updates, data storage and processing, AI model training, and cybersecurity measures. The use of advanced technologies like AI and blockchain can be expensive but is essential for robust compliance solutions.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: RegTech platforms are expected to grow as regulatory complexity increases and organizations seek more efficient ways to manage compliance. The market is likely to see continued innovation in AI, blockchain, and other technologies that can further automate and enhance compliance processes.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by jurisdiction, but common requirements include Know Your Customer (KYC), Anti-Money Laundering (AML) regulations, and data privacy laws. Compliance with these regulations is critical for the adoption of RegTech platforms.
ai.risks: Risks associated with RegTech include cybersecurity threats, regulatory changes that may affect platform functionality, and the potential for AI bias in decision-making processes. Ensuring robust security measures and regular updates to comply with new regulations are crucial.
ai.profitability: Profitability is driven by subscription fees, transaction-based commissions, and value-added services offered by RegTech providers. The market has shown growth potential due to increasing regulatory demands and the need for efficient compliance solutions.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments in RegTech may include more advanced AI capabilities, integration with other financial technologies (fintech), and the expansion of use cases beyond traditional financial services into sectors like healthcare and retail.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and data center operations. AI models require significant computational power but can be optimized for efficiency.

glossary.def: Short for Regulatory Technology, it refers to software solutions that automate regulatory compliance processes in financial services and other industries.
A branch of computer science that focuses on creating systems capable of performing tasks requiring human-like intelligence, such as data analysis and pattern recognition.
A decentralized digital ledger technology that provides a secure, transparent, and immutable record-keeping system for transactions or other activities.

subsystems.name: Data ingestion and entity resolution
subsystems.role: pulls transaction, trading, client and ownership data out of core systems and stitches it together.
parts: connectors to core banking, trading and payment systems
Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) mapping and deduplication

subsystems.name: Regulatory change monitoring
subsystems.role: watches regulators' publications and flags what actually changed.

subsystems.name: Detection and screening analytics
subsystems.role: finds suspicious patterns rather than just checking boxes.
parts: graph analytics over ownership and payment networks

subsystems.name: Reporting and submission
subsystems.role: assembles and files the reports regulators require.

subsystems.name: Case management and workflow
subsystems.role: humans review, escalate and sign off on what the machine flags.

subsystems.name: Audit trail and explainability
subsystems.role: lets an examiner reconstruct exactly why a decision was made.
parts: reason codes for every automated decision

buildSteps.title: Map the obligations
buildSteps.detail: Legal analysts and engineers read the applicable rules and break them into discrete, testable obligations with owners and evidence requirements.

buildSteps.title: Model the data
buildSteps.detail: Decide which fields each obligation needs, then build connectors that extract and normalise them — including reference data such as legal entity identifiers.

buildSteps.title: Write the rules as code
buildSteps.detail: Obligations become decision tables and rule sets in a versioned repository, each backed by test cases drawn from real scenarios.

buildSteps.title: Train and tune the detection models
buildSteps.detail: Anomaly and screening models are fitted on historical data, then thresholds are set to balance missed cases against alert volume, and results are back-tested.

buildSteps.title: Build the reporting pipeline
buildSteps.detail: Report templates, validation rules and submission interfaces are implemented against the regulator's published schema and tested end to end.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the audit trail
buildSteps.detail: Logging is added so every flag, score and override is recorded with its inputs, model version and reason code.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and harden
buildSteps.detail: APIs connect the platform to core systems; access control, encryption and monitoring are applied, since the data is among the most sensitive a firm holds.

buildSteps.title: Validate and gain acceptance
buildSteps.detail: Internal audit and, often, the supervisor review the logic and evidence before the platform is relied on for live filings.

prerequisites.why: the Legal Entity Identifier, ISO 20022 messaging and XBRL tagging give machines something unambiguous to join and file on.
compliance workloads need elastic compute and clean interfaces into legacy core systems.
extracting obligations from dense regulatory prose is doable but still needs human confirmation.

prerequisites.tech: Explainable machine learning and model risk management
prerequisites.why: a model that cannot justify its alerts will not survive supervisory scrutiny.
sharing risk signals across institutions without pooling raw customer data needs techniques like secure aggregation or zero-knowledge proofs.

pathway.milestone: cloud-based platforms automating reporting, sanctions screening and transaction monitoring
pathway.unlocks: lower compliance cost per client and faster filing cycles.

pathway.milestone: machine-readable regulation, with rules published in structured form and adopted directly by firms
pathway.unlocks: less manual translation between legal text and code, and fewer interpretation gaps.

pathway.milestone: supervisory technology using the same data feeds, moving from periodic reports to near-continuous oversight
pathway.unlocks: problems surfaced earlier and smaller remediation bills.

pathway.milestone: cross-border data sharing under agreed privacy safeguards, with cryptographic proofs instead of raw record exchange
pathway.unlocks: detection of flows that cross jurisdictions and currently fall between regulators.
